item.title: Demystifying macOS Platform SSO: How Apple and Microsoft Entra ID work together
item.description:
Platform SSO has been transforming the macOS sign-in experience by bringing Microsoft Entra authentication closer to the operating system. Users can sign in to their Mac and access work applications with fewer authentication prompts, while organizations retain Microsoft Entra device trust and access controls.

As more organizations deploy Platform SSO, new questions have emerged:

  • What actually happens under the hood?
  • Which responsibilities belong to Apple, and which belong to Microsoft?
  • Where are credentials created and protected?
  • Does every application receive the Platform SSO Primary Refresh Token (PRT)?

To help answer these questions, we published a new Microsoft Learn article: Architecture and authentication flow for macOS Platform SSO with Microsoft Entra ID.

Apple Platform SSO is an extensible framework that can work with supported identity-provider extensions. This post focuses on its integration with Microsoft Entra ID through the Microsoft Enterprise SSO plug-in. It provides a practical mental model, highlights the ownership boundaries between Apple and Microsoft, and walks through the key parts of the architecture.

Why the ownership boundary can be difficult to see

From the user's perspective, Platform SSO can feel like one continuous experience. The Mac is enrolled, the user completes registration, and supported applications begin signing in with fewer prompts.

Behind that experience, however, several systems retain distinct responsibilities. MDM (Mobile Device Management) deploys the Platform SSO policy. The Microsoft Enterprise SSO plug-in connects the Mac to Microsoft Entra ID. macOS owns the operating-system experience and protects the platform credentials. Microsoft Entra ID validates the authentication proofs and issues identity credentials. Applications consume only the authorization intended for them.

Platform SSO is a shared architecture across device management, Apple, and Microsoft. The following diagram shows how responsibilities are divided across the end-to-end flow.

Ownership boundaries in macOS Platform SSO with Microsoft Entra ID.

This division of responsibility isn't just an implementation detail. It establishes the security boundaries that allow Platform SSO to reduce authentication prompts without distributing powerful credentials to every application.

Three ideas that make the architecture easier to understand

item.description:
AI and agents are changing the access landscape at a pace that challenges even mature identity and security programs. Without centralized visibility and control, agent sprawl risks becoming shadow IT at a scale we've never had to manage before.

AI amplifies today's identity challenges. Every agent needs an identity, the right access, and controls that adapt as risk changes.
We're designing Microsoft Entra for this reality: secure access for every identity, human or agent, to every resource, from anywhere.

This week at Microsoft Ignite, we're announcing new Microsoft Entra capabilities, advancing this strategy around three customer priorities: strengthen your identity foundation, secure agent access at scale, and turn customer identity into a competitive advantage.

Strengthen your identity foundation

Agent adoption makes strengthening the identity foundation more urgent.
Agents inherit unnecessary privileges, persistent access, and weak governance. Today's identity backlog becomes tomorrow's agent security problem.

As one practitioner told us, “If you're not doing it for humans today, you're going to struggle with agents.”

Make every sign-in phishing-resistant and verified

Secure access starts with phishing-resistant credentials like passkeys, now the default for new accounts in Microsoft Entra. Yet 57% of organizations still rely on phishable authentication methods.[i] Weaker credentials like SMS codes leave users vulnerable to adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing attacks, which target not only sign-ins, but also onboarding and account recovery.

  • High assurance credentials (preview). A strong credential is only as trustworthy as the process used to issue and recover it. item.description:

Instead of managing dozens of individual policies, policy plans let you define your access intent once and enforce it consistently across every identity. item.title: AI agents are coming—are your identity controls prepared?
item.description:
AI is reshaping identity risk. Attackers now use AI to automate phishing, social engineering, and privilege escalation, making credential theft faster and more convincing than ever. SMS codes and push approvals can be intercepted, while standing privileges give attackers reach far beyond a single account.

On the other hand, as organizations adopt AI agents, identity risk grows exponentially. Securing agent identities is critical to maintaining trust and control. The same principles that protect user identities must now extend to every agent identity.

Reinforcing the principles

Microsoft’s recently published guidance, Secure identity to get ready for AI, reinforces key principles for securing identities: move users and administrators to phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), eliminate standing privileges with Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM), and extend a unified policy engine to govern every identity.

Putting the principles into practice

Implement these principles in sequence to strengthen your Zero Trust foundation and secure every identity, starting with the accounts and controls you already manage:

  • Move users and admins to phishing-resistant MFA. Protect privileged accounts first by requiring MFA for every administrator and moving them to device-bound passkeys or FIDO2 security keys. Plan a phishing-resistant, passwordless authentication rollout across your workforce using methods such as Windows Hello for Business, device-bound passkeys, synced passkeys, or certificate-based authentication.
  • Eliminate standing privileges. Permanent administrative assignments create lasting exposure. Run Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) discovery, and convert static roles to eligible, time-bound activations that require justification and MFA. Govern guest access through expiring access packages.
  • Apply policy coverage across every identity and resource. Apply Conditional Access broadly, block legacy authentication, and require device compliance through Microsoft Intune. Enable Microsoft Entra ID Protection to respond to identity risk in real time by enforcing MFA at medium risk and a credential reset at high risk. Maintain continuous coverage by exporting logs to Microsoft Sentinel or Azure Monitor, alerting on privileged activations, and running recurring access reviews.

Start your secure identity journey today

Phishing-resistant MFA removes the password and SMS-based paths attackers depend on. Just-in-time activation through PIM removes standing privileges. item.title: Why identity needs network insight to make Zero Trust work
item.description:
Your users sign in successfully—and then what? The session can be hijacked, device posture can degrade, and traffic to non-federated SaaS and AI apps can slip past the identity controls you trust to protect them. That’s the gap admins see every day: identity tells you who, but not what’s happening across the network during the session—and it’s why identity alone can’t carry Zero Trust on its own.

Most Zero Trust strategies start with identity—and for good reason. Identity is the control point for authenticating users and granting access. But identity by itself can’t address every evolving risk. Today, users connect from anywhere, on any device, and interact with thousands of apps across cloud, AI, internet, and private networks. The gap between identity and network security creates blind spots that attackers can exploit.

Microsoft’s approach is clear: identity is most effective when it operates with full awareness of the network. That’s why Microsoft Entra brings identity and network protections together in a unified architecture designed for modern Zero Trust security.

Why identity alone is not enough

Traditional access decisions often stop at sign-in and rely on credentials plus multifactor authentication. This works for many scenarios—but not all. In practice, a session that looks low-risk at sign-in can turn risky minutes later, and unmanaged traffic to AI tools and non-federated SaaS apps creates blind spots your identity policies weren’t designed to cover Why? Because threats don’t disappear after a successful sign-in:

  • Risk changes dynamically: A user’s session can be hijacked, or device posture can deteriorate mid-session.
  • Blind spots in traffic: Connections to non-federated SaaS apps or AI services often bypass identity controls.
  • Static policies fail: Network contexts like location or traffic path often go unchecked.

Zero Trust isn’t just about verifying identity at the front door—it’s about making continuous, adaptive decisions that factor in identity, device, network conditions, and session context together.

How Microsoft Entra unifies identity and network signals

Microsoft brings these controls together through a single security architecture anchored by Microsoft Entra ID, Conditional Access, continuous access evaluation, and Global Secure Access, including Microsoft Entra Internet Access and Microsoft Entra Private Access.

Key principles

  • Conditional Access as a unified engine

item.title: Designing smarter access policies for hybrid enterprises
item.description:
Every hybrid enterprise eventually reaches the same point: the security model that worked when everyone was inside the corporate network no longer holds up when people, apps, and data are distributed across clouds, data centers, and unmanaged devices. Add AI agents acting on users’ behalf, and the idea of a trusted perimeter loses even more relevance. The answer is not more controls for their own sake, but better-designed policies: deliberate rules that determine who and what can access specific resources, under which conditions, and how access adapts as risk changes. Get the design right, and security becomes an enabler rather than a burden. Get it wrong, and you either leave gaps attackers can exploit or frustrate the users you are trying to protect. This article explains how to get it right.

TL;DR

In a hybrid enterprise, users, apps, and data no longer sit behind a single perimeter, and AI agents also make access requests. This article explains how to design Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies and policy governance for that reality, protecting what matters without slowing people down. The goal is a Zero Trust posture you can operate, not merely deploy.

Why this matters

Hybrid work is no longer a transition state; it is the operating model. Most organizations now run apps across multiple clouds, maintain legacy systems on-premises, and support a distributed workforce that expects access to feel immediate and seamless. That combination creates real tension in policy design: policies that are too loose leave gaps, while policies that are too rigid lock out the people they are meant to enable.

Organizations that get this right treat policy as a design discipline rather than a collection of rules. A Zero Trust architecture is not measured by how many controls you enable. It is measured by how well those controls adapt to how people actually work. Good policy design keeps security strong and friction low, distinguishing a framework people trust from one they work around.

Start with identity, not the network

In a hybrid environment, identity is the perimeter. Network location reveals little about whether a request is safe, so policies should begin with who the user is, how they authenticate, and what the available signals indicate about the session.

Practically, that means requiring multi-factor authentication for everyone and moving toward phishing-resistant methods as your baseline rather than your aspiration. It also means evaluating each sign-in in context, factoring in user risk and session conditions instead of granting standing access. For privileged accounts, replace always-on admin rights with just-in-time elevation through Privileged Identity Management, so elevated access exists only for as long as the task requires it.

item.title: Sign in to Microsoft apps with passkeys from external identity providers
item.description:
Organizations that use an external identity provider to authenticate Microsoft 365 users can now extend browser-based passkeys, security keys, and eligible single sign-on sessions to supported Microsoft app sign-ins—including Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Microsoft To Do—on Android, iOS, and managed macOS.

Previously, some Microsoft app sign-ins used an embedded web view that couldn’t provide the browser capabilities required to support passkeys (FIDO2) issued by external identity providers. As a result, some users couldn’t use a passkey or security key or complete sign-in when the identity provider required passkeys or blocked embedded web views.

Browser authentication for external identity providers addresses this limitation by opening only the external identity provider step in the system browser. After authentication, the user returns to the Microsoft identity broker—the trusted Microsoft component that coordinates app sign-in—and the originating app completes sign-in.

 

Browser authentication opens the external identity provider’s sign-in step in the system browser.

Extend your passkey strategy to Microsoft app sign-ins

Organizations federated through WS-Fed or SAML 2.0 can use this capability to extend supported external identity provider authentication methods to Microsoft app sign-ins. Users can authenticate with passkeys or FIDO2 security keys in the system browser, and eligible browser sessions can reduce repeated prompts.

With this capability, you can:

  • Use external identity provider passkeys and FIDO2 security keys. The external identity provider authentication step runs in a browser surface that supports WebAuthn, so users can use FIDO credentials registered with that identity provider instead of falling back to a password-only experience.
  • Enable single sign-on from native apps to web apps. The system browser provides a shared web surface and can reuse an eligible identity provider session, reducing unnecessary sign-in prompts.
  • Support identity providers that reject embedded web views. Organizations can maintain identity provider policies that require a system browser without creating a separate authentication path for supported Microsoft apps.
  • Roll out with platform-level control. Administrators enable the experience in the relevant federation configuration and select the platforms where it applies.

This creates a more consistent experience across web and supported Microsoft app sign-ins without requiring a separate authentication approach for embedded sign-in surfaces.

Keep the brokered app experience

item.title: Public preview of self-service onboarding for new Microsoft Entra App Gallery applications
item.description:
Previously, publishing a new application to Microsoft Entra App Gallery could require multiple review cycles. Publishers submitted an integration, received feedback, made corrections, and resubmitted it, which delayed when customers could discover and deploy the application.

Today, we're announcing the public preview of self-service onboarding for new applications to Microsoft Entra App Gallery.

The new experience helps independent software vendors validate supported integrations before submission, resolve common configuration issues earlier, and manage publishing through a guided workflow in the Microsoft Entra admin center. Publishers can create a new App Gallery submission, associate validation results, provide customer-facing documentation and logos, submit the application for Microsoft review, and track its status throughout the process.

Validate before submitting

Configuration issues that previously surfaced during Microsoft review can now be identified earlier.

With self-service onboarding, publishers can test supported integrations against Microsoft Entra App Gallery requirements before submission, while they still have the context needed to address identified issues.

The public preview supports validation for the following.

Capability

Validation experience

OIDC single-tenant and multitenant SSO

Microsoft Entra App Validator browser extension

SAML SSO

Microsoft Entra App Validator browser extension

User provisioning

Microsoft-provided Logic Apps validation flow or SCIM onboarding agent

For OIDC and SAML integrations, the Microsoft Entra App Validator guides publishers through the required sign-in scenarios, identifies blocking issues, and generates the Test ID needed for submission. For user provisioning, Microsoft-provided validation tools test the integration and generate validation results that can be associated with the App Gallery submission.

 

The Microsoft Entra App Validator helps publishers identify configuration issues in new OIDC and SAML integrations before submission.

item.title: Replace VPN access with identity-driven security
item.description:
Traditional VPNs no longer fit the security or agility needs of modern enterprises. Static tunnels, device trust assumptions, and network-level access introduce risk in a Zero Trust world.

Microsoft Entra Private Access offers a different path. As a component of Global Secure Access, it is designed to replace traditional VPN access to private resources with identity-driven, per-app connectivity. That distinction matters: Global Secure Access is the broader Security Service Edge framework, while Microsoft Entra Private Access is the component most directly aligned to VPN replacement for private applications.

This guide provides a practical, phased strategy to replace VPN with identity-driven, secure access services provided by Microsoft Entra Private Access.

Start here:

  • Plan and operate your Global Secure Access deployment
  • Use the Global Secure Access operations guide

Why replace VPN now

As organizations embrace hybrid work, cloud services, and Zero Trust security models, VPNs often become a source of both security and operational challenges. By design, VPNs extend network connectivity to remote users, frequently providing access to more resources than necessary. This approach conflicts with the principle of least privilege and increases the potential impact of compromised accounts or devices.

VPN infrastructure can also create operational overhead. Organizations must maintain gateways, manage capacity, monitor performance, and address availability concerns. Split-tunnel configurations, while often necessary for performance, can introduce visibility gaps that attackers can exploit.

At the same time, attackers continue to target remote access infrastructure using stolen credentials, phishing campaigns, and MFA fatigue attacks. Replacing VPNs with identity-driven access reduces the attack surface, enforces granular access controls, and delivers a more seamless experience for users

Read more: Identity Under Attack: How AI Learns to Defend

Step 1: Understand your private application landscape

A successful VPN modernization project begins with visibility. Start by identifying the private applications, file shares, and internal web resources that currently rely on VPN connectivity. Understanding who uses these resources, from where, and on what devices will help determine migration priorities.

Organizations should evaluate workloads based on factors such as business criticality, sensitivity of data, user impact, and overall migration complexity. Applications supporting functions such as finance, HR, or other sensitive business processes often benefit most from early plan [truncated]

item.title: Simplify Employee Identity Lifecycle with HiBob and Microsoft Entra
item.description:
Every workforce transition creates an identity moment that your IT team must get right. That’s why we’re excited to announce the general availability of HiBob’s native integration with Microsoft Entra. It helps you turn trusted workforce changes in HiBob into governed identity actions, so employees get the right access across on-premises and cloud apps as they join, change roles, or leave.

Why this matters

New hires need accounts and the right access from day one. When employees change roles, their access needs to change with them. And when someone leaves, that access needs to be removed quickly. Manual handoffs, tickets, and custom integrations slow these moments down, create more work for IT, and add unnecessary security risk. Connecting trusted workforce data in HiBob with Microsoft Entra helps you securely govern and automate the process, reducing the back-and-forth.

If your organization uses HiBob, this integration gives your HR and IT teams a more connected way to manage identity changes across hybrid environments. HR keeps workforce information current in HiBob, while IT decides how Microsoft Entra applies mappings, scoping rules, provisioning policies, and governance controls. Together, the systems turn workforce events into consistent identity actions - reducing manual handoffs, speeding up lifecycle processes, and creating a stronger foundation for identity governance.

Modernize identity without forcing a disruptive migration

Many organizations are moving applications and infrastructure to the cloud while still supporting on-premises directories. Modernizing identity does not mean replacing everything at once. The HiBob integration works with the environment you have today and helps you move toward a more cloud-managed model over time.

This integration advances a broader Microsoft Entra strategy: bring identity lifecycle control, visibility, and governance into a unified cloud service. Microsoft Entra can serve as the control plane for workforce identity changes across hybrid and cloud environments, while IT retains control over which users are in scope, how attributes are mapped, and what actions are performed.

item.title: Instant revocation of service principal bearer tokens with CAE
item.description:
Introduction

Workload identities such as service principals are an important part of the attack surface in Entra: they are often used by critical automated processes, and they can carry privileged and sensitive permissions. The authentication flow used by these principals is the Client Credential flow, which results in an access token.

In this blog post, I'll describe how Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) can be leveraged to instantly invalidate an access token for a service principal in Microsoft Entra. This is incredibly valuable as part of a kill-switch in incident response scenarios.

Access tokens (aka bearer tokens)

Access tokens are bearer tokens. Instant invalidation of bearer tokens is an important response capability because normally these tokens have a lifetime between 60 and 90 minutes.

This is a long time in scenarios where a compromised token can be used for triggering malicious automation by a bad actor.

How to enable CAE for service principal tokens

CAE is enabled by a “client capability” claim, “xms_cc”, with the value of “cp1”.

The screenshot below shows an example of a PowerShell function that incorporates this:

Recognizing a CAE-enabled token 

The access token I get back from this request is base64 encoded. I can echo this encoded value back in my PowerShell session, then paste it into a decoder to investigate it (jwt.io or jwt.ms).

The first thing you will notice is the presence of this claim:

The second thing you will notice is the lifetime of the token:

The expiry value is now (roughly) 24 hours after the “iat” (issued at) time, instead of the 60-90 minutes that we normally see in tokens that are not CAE-enabled.

Why does this matter

Although a longer lifetime seems less secure, Microsoft’s philosophy around this is that with Workload Identity Protection enabled, risk levels can dynamically be picked up for the identity.

If an identity is at a high risk level, the token is revoked within a couple of minutes automatically.

High risk is only one of three revocation events. At the time of writing, the revocation events are:

  • Service Principal at high risk
  • Service Principal disabled
  • Service Principal deleted
